description: Black box probe results for the router, hosts, one IoT device and two external control targets. Built from the probe metrics this blackbox exporter actually publishes.

panels.description: Six targets are configured: the router, two hosts, one IoT device and two external controls.
panels.title: Probes up

panels.description: vector(0) makes this read 0 rather than No data when everything is healthy.
panels.title: Probes down

panels.description: Proportion rather than count, so it survives adding targets.
panels.title: Availability now

panels.description: The single most useful panel here. If this is up while a device is down, the problem is the device. If everything is down together, the problem is your network or the exporter.
panels.title: External control

panels.description: The flap leader. A device that transitions constantly is a dashboard candidate, not a paging candidate.
panels.title: Most unstable target, 24h

panels.description: Slowest probe of the moment.
panels.title: Worst latency now

panels.description: One bar per target. Red is down. Grouped by job in the legend labels.
panels.title: Probe status by target

panels.description: Seconds since each target last answered. More actionable during an incident than a binary up or down.
panels.title: Time since last seen up

panels.description: Flat at 1 is healthy. Use a narrow time range to tell a 30 second flap apart from a real outage; at a wide range they look identical, which is why alert rules need a for clause.
panels.title: Probe success over time

panels.description: Retention is 6h, so this currently averages over whatever history exists rather than a true 24 hours.
panels.title: Availability, last 24h

panels.description: The flap counter. Counts transitions in both directions, so one outage with a recovery scores 2.
panels.title: State changes, last 24h

panels.description: Total probe time across every phase. Wi-Fi power saving on battery devices shows as periodic spikes.
panels.title: Probe latency

panels.description: Broken down by phase: resolve, setup and rtt. The rtt phase is the actual network latency.
panels.title: ICMP round trip

panels.description: TTL on the reply, so it shows how many hops away each target is. The router is one hop; 1.1.1.1 is many. A sudden change means the route changed, which almost nobody dashboards.
panels.title: Hops to target

panels.description: 4 or 6. Worth watching because a probe silently falling back to IPv6 produces confusing results, which is why ip_protocol_fallback is disabled in the blackbox config.
panels.title: IP protocol used

panels.description: Green from 200, amber for redirects, red for 4xx and 5xx. A 200 from the wrong page still counts as success, which is what probe_failed_due_to_regex exists to catch.
panels.title: HTTP status code

panels.description: Phases: resolve, connect, tls, processing, transfer. This is the curl timing breakdown as a panel, and it tells you which layer to fix.
panels.title: HTTP phase breakdown

panels.description: A sudden change in body size often means the page changed to an error or a login redirect while still returning 200.
panels.title: Response size

panels.description: Catches a site quietly starting to redirect, which adds latency and can break API clients.
panels.title: Redirects followed

panels.description: 1.1 or 2.0. A downgrade usually means a proxy or load balancer changed.
panels.title: HTTP version

panels.description: 1 means the page returned successfully but did not contain the expected content. No regex is configured yet, so this reads 0 for every target.
panels.title: Content regex failure

panels.description: HTTPS targets only. Certificate expiry is a classic outage cause precisely because nothing warns you until it happens.
panels.title: Days until certificate expiry

panels.description: A sawtooth means automated renewal is working. A straight line to zero means it is not.
panels.title: Certificate expiry over time

panels.description: Whether the final request used TLS. A target silently dropping to plain HTTP after a redirect shows here.
panels.title: TLS in use

panels.description: The version label carries the result. A downgrade is a compliance signal worth noticing.
panels.title: TLS version negotiated

panels.description: Issuer and subject of the served chain. A changed issuer means the certificate was reissued, possibly by something you did not expect.
panels.title: Certificate chain

panels.description: Only targets given as hostnames produce this. Raw IP targets have nothing to resolve, so four of the six are absent by design.
panels.title: DNS lookup time

panels.description: probe_ip_addr_hash is a hash of the resolved address. A change means DNS now points somewhere else, which catches a DHCP reassignment or a CDN switch before anything breaks.
panels.title: Target IP changes

panels.description: The hash itself is meaningless; only changes matter. Compare against the panel to the left.
panels.title: Current resolved address hash

panels.description: If the exporter stops, every probe series disappears rather than going to 0. That silent failure is why the alert rule uses absent().
panels.title: Blackbox exporter reachable

panels.description: A probe job approaching the 15s scrape interval means timeouts are being hit.
panels.title: Scrape duration, probe jobs

panels.description: Rising duration precedes probes starting to fail.
panels.title: Probe job scrape duration

panels.description: Every target with its current state, filterable by job. The one table to read first during an incident.
panels.title: All probe results now
